app_id: The Great Army lands in East Anglia

research_claim: Fraction 0.5 is staging. The attested timing is two nights after relief of London, after the Sherston encounter and before Assandun; no fixed day or month is recorded.
source_title: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, Ingram/Giles composite English translation
note: The Chronicle supports a relative sequence only. Both episode dateNotes explicitly say the day and month are unknown; fraction 0.5 is staging, not a claimed date.

research_claim: 1014 is the saga framing, not a secure event date from the Chronicle. The Chronicle records repeated attacks in 1009–10 and Æthelred’s return in 1014, without bridge demolition.

research_claim: The event is attested but this point is a candidate localization. The Chronicle does not identify a modern coordinate; render a disputed candidate, not a fixed battlefield.
source_title: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, Ingram/Giles composite English translation

app_claim: "Founded in 635 from Iona. Cuthbert died here in 687 and the Lindisfarne Gospels were made about 710-725. Raided on 8 June 793, left for good in 875, and refounded as a cell of Durham by 1122 until its closure in 1537."
research_claim: Cuthbert died on Farne, not at Lindisfarne. His burial was at Lindisfarne. The app’s “died here” conflates death and burial.
source_title: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of England, translated A. M. Sellar (1907)
note: Bede IV.29 and the Farne history distinguish death on Farne from burial at Lindisfarne.

research_claim: The scalar end 1063 should support an alternative 1064 end as already acknowledged in the app note. Store Hudson and Jones as competing chronology claims.
note: The revised DWB article argues 1064; the current app note already preserves that alternative alongside conventional 1063. This does not justify replacing 1063 outright.

app_claim: "Hywel held Seisyllwg from 920 and Dyfed by marriage, and on the death of Idwal Foel in 942 took Gwynedd (and with it Powys), ruling all Wales except Morgannwg and Gwent until his death in 950. The Welsh law-books are attributed to him, though no manuscript is earlier than the 13th century. His kingdom broke up at his death."
research_claim: The statement that no law manuscript predates the thirteenth century conflicts with DWB’s late-twelfth-century earliest manuscript; attribution of the law collection to Hywel is not contemporary documentation.
note: DWB explicitly dates the oldest manuscript to the last quarter of the twelfth century.

research_claim: 674 dates Wearmouth; Jarrow followed c.681–682 and was dedicated 23 April 685. Separate place/structure phases avoid making the Jarrow marker appear in 674.
source_title: Anglo-Saxon England: a bibliographical handbook for students of Anglo-Saxon history
note: The Cambridge handbook dates the two sites separately. The problem is the Jarrow marker’s 674 onset, not denial that Wearmouth was founded in 674.

research_claim: 654 cannot mean the first existence of Northumbria as a united kingship: Edwin and Oswald ruled both components before it, with intervening divisions. Use successive polity phases.
source_title: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of England, translated A. M. Sellar (1907)
note: Bede and EH attest earlier Northumbrian unions. A continuous 654 start loses Edwin and Oswald.

app_claim: "Rhodri became king of Gwynedd in 844, took Powys in 855 and Seisyllwg in 872, so that for a few years one king ruled most of Wales outside the south-east and Dyfed. He was killed fighting the English; the Dictionary of Welsh Biography gives 877, other reckonings 878. His sons divided the lands. No boundary is drawn because none is known."
research_claim: Thornton qualifies Rhodri’s control of Powys as possible in 855 or later; the app’s “took Powys in 855” is too definite. Death chronology remains 877 versus 878.
source_title: Rhodri Mawr (b. before 844, d. 878), king of Gwynedd
note: Thornton’s accessible ODNB extract uses possible control in 855 or later. The overstatement recurs in two polity notes.

research_claim: The archaeological camp is on the high ground north of Torksey, mostly Brampton parish, centred on HER grid SK836802. A village marker is not the camp centroid.
source_title: MLI125067: Winter Camp of the Viking Great Army at Torksey
note: HER gives the northern camp and estimated centre. Moving the shared town/camp point would misplace later phases; identify it as a town reference and add a separate camp feature.

research_claim: 867 is a display placeholder. English Heritage explicitly says abandonment occurred at an unknown point in the ninth century. Preserve a bounded uncertain end.
note: EH explicitly denies knowledge of the precise ninth-century abandonment.

app_claim: "Roman Venta, refounded by Alfred with a new street grid and the largest burh in the Burghal Hidage. It was second only to London at Domesday but thirtieth in the 1377 poll tax."
research_claim: The Hidage assessment is 2,400 hides for Winchester, also 2,400 for Wallingford and appended Warwick. These fiscal figures do not by themselves establish an exclusive largest-town ranking or population.
source_title: The Burghal Hidage: the establishment of a text
note: The edition gives Winchester and Wallingford equal 2,400-hide assessments, not exclusive population rank.

app_claim: [{"from": 995, "to": 1092, "label": "Shrine of St Cuthbert on the river peninsula", "size": 3}, {"from": 1093, "to": 1539, "label": "Norman cathedral, castle and seat of the prince-bishops", "size": 4}, {"from": 1540, "to": null, "label": "Cathedral city of a county palatine", "size": 3}]

app_claim: Date (14 May 1264) confirmed by the Battlefields Trust, which describes the site as securely located on the north side of the town. Historic England registers it as 'Battle of Lewes 1264' (list entry 1000018).

note: Coflein’s northern narrative conflicts with its Templeton catalogue point. No replacement exact coordinate is established.

app_claim: Timber halls start in 411, abandonment in 520.

app_claim: Settlement spans 2550–2451 BCE; henge follows in 2450.

note: EH states duration unknown and soil/settlement change, not a climate-caused 800 BCE abandonment.

app_claim: Contraction phase begins 351 CE.

app_claim: Province starts exactly in 197.

app_claim: Horse begins at 1000 BCE; later phase starts 700 BCE.

app_claim: "The monastery founded by St David in the 6th century became the leading church of Wales and, under Norman bishops from 1115, a cathedral.
